idiom_name: function template over std::unordered_map with find + emplace
implementation_notes: std::unordered_map (C++11) is the store and a small function template is the wrapper; use find() plus emplace() rather than operator[], because operator[] default-constructs the mapped value and inserts an entry on every lookup, which defeats the purpose for expensive values. Store or capture the map where its lifetime belongs (a member for per-object memos, a function-local static or a dedicated struct for process-wide ones) and return a copy or a reference from the entry rather than an iterator that a later rehash can invalidate - the standard guarantees that references and pointers to an element are invalidated only by erasing that element, while iterators are invalidated by rehashing. The container replaces the classic hand-written table; the manual table is still justified only when the key domain is dense and integer-valued or when allocation must be avoided entirely.
pitfalls: operator[] on the cache default-constructs and inserts on every probe, so a lookup that should miss silently grows the map.
Values must be movable and keys hashable/equality-comparable; a mutable key whose hash changes leaves an entry that can no longer be found.

A member-function memo has no thread safety of its own: concurrent calls race on the same map, and a single mutex around the wrapper serializes all misses and can deadlock if the memoized work recurses into it.
Unordered iteration plus an eviction policy is easy to get wrong: erase() during iteration invalidates only the erased iterator, but rehash invalidates all of them.

variants.name: C++17 try_emplace memo (no wasted construction)
variants.implementation_notes: try_emplace (C++17) inserts only when the key is absent and does nothing otherwise, and unlike insert/emplace it does not move from rvalue arguments when the insertion does not happen - which makes it the correct primitive for caches of move-only values such as unique_ptr and for keys that are expensive to copy. The wrapper becomes a two-line lookup with one insertion attempt; C++20 adds contains() for a cheap presence test and transparent hashers for heterogeneous lookup, which avoids materialising a temporary key object on every probe. It replaces the find-then-emplace pair of the C++11 variant with one call; the C++11 form is still correct and remains the choice when the toolchain cannot move to C++17.
pitfalls: try_emplace evaluates the mapped value's constructor arguments eagerly, so an expensive argument expression is still computed before the call; wrap the computation in a lambda or check presence first when the hit path must be free.
The pair of iterators returned by insertion is invalidated by rehashing, so do not cache iterators across insertions.
It is a member of the container, not a memo facility: capacity, eviction and thread safety are still yours to design.

variants.name: Dense index table for integer domains (classic DP tabulation)
variants.idiom_name: std::vector value table plus a separate computed bitmap
variants.implementation_notes: When the argument is a dense integer index, the hash map is the wrong structure: a std::vector indexed by the argument is constant-time with no hashing, no allocation per entry and no rehash, and a parallel std::vector<char> (or vector<bool>) records which slots are computed, so a legitimate zero result is still a hit. This is tabulation rather than a wrapper - the memoized function takes the table as part of its state, which is why the classic structure is still justified here: bottom-up or top-down DP over a compact index range is faster and more predictable than any general store, but it does not generalise to structured or sparse keys.
pitfalls: The table must be sized before the recursion starts; resizing during computation invalidates references held by callers.
Without the separate computed flag a zero result is indistinguishable from an unvisited slot and the function recurses forever on that key.
Plain vectors are not thread-safe and not shared: the table is per-call or per-object state, and sharing one across threads needs external synchronisation.
Recursion depth is bounded by the index range, so a dense table trades key-domain assumptions for stack usage.
